content: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is a condition characterized by episodes of complete cessation of breathing (apnoea) or insufficient breathing (hypopnoea) during sleep. Men with OSA often experience symptoms such as snoring, poor-quality sleep, and excessive daytime sleepiness. In contrast, women tend to report less specific symptoms, including fatigue, low energy, difficulty falling asleep, and morning headaches. OSA is associated with an increased risk of occupational injuries, metabolic and cardiovascular diseases, mortality, and traffic accidents. The primary treatment for OSA is continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), which involves a machine delivering constant air pressure through a mask or nosepiece. However, adherence to CPAP therapy is often suboptimal. Myofunctional therapy, which involves oropharyngeal exercises targeting the mouth, throat, and upper airway muscles, has been proposed as an alternative treatment. These exercises include isotonic and isometric activities aimed at improving functions such as speaking, breathing, blowing, sucking, chewing, and swallowing. A systematic review evaluated the benefits and harms of myofunctional therapy for OSA. Nine randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 347 participants (69 women and 13 children) were included. The participants' mean age ranged from 46 to 51 years, and the severity of OSA varied from mild to severe. The studies lasted between two and four months. None of the studies reported outcomes related to accidents, cardiovascular diseases, or mortality, and no adverse events were documented. In adults, compared to sham therapy, myofunctional therapy likely reduces daytime sleepiness, as measured by the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), with a mean difference (MD) of -4.52 points (moderate-certainty evidence). It may also improve sleep quality (MD -3.90 points; low-certainty evidence) and significantly reduce the Apnoea-Hypopnoea Index (AHI) (MD -13.20 points; low-certainty evidence). However, its effect on snoring frequency is uncertain, and it likely only slightly reduces subjective snoring intensity (MD -1.9 points; moderate-certainty evidence). When compared to a waiting list, myofunctional therapy may reduce daytime sleepiness (ESS MD -3.00 points; low-certainty evidence) and AHI (MD -6.20 points; low-certainty evidence), but it may have little to no effect on sleep quality (MD -0.70 points; low-certainty evidence). Compared to CPAP, myofunctional therapy may result in little to no difference in daytime sleepiness (MD 0.30 points; low-certainty evidence) but may increase AHI (MD 9.60 points; low-certainty evidence). When compared to CPAP combined with myofunctional therapy, myofunctional therapy alone may result in little to no difference in daytime sleepiness (MD 0.20 points; low-certainty evidence) but may increase AHI (MD 10.50 points; low-certainty evidence). Compared to respiratory exercises combined with a nasal dilator strip, myofunctional therapy may result in little to no difference in daytime sleepiness (MD 0.20 points; low-certainty evidence) but likely slightly improves sleep quality (MD -1.94 points; moderate-certainty evidence). It may have little to no effect on AHI (MD -3.80 points; low-certainty evidence). Compared to standard medical treatment, myofunctional therapy may reduce daytime sleepiness (MD -6.40 points; low-certainty evidence) and may improve sleep quality (MD -3.10 points; low-certainty evidence). In children, when compared to nasal washing alone, the combination of myofunctional therapy and nasal washing may result in little to no difference in AHI (MD 3.00 points; low-certainty evidence). The authors concluded that myofunctional therapy likely reduces daytime sleepiness and may improve sleep quality in the short term when compared to sham therapy. However, the certainty of the evidence ranges from moderate to very low due to limitations such as lack of blinding, incomplete data, and imprecision. Further research is needed, with larger sample sizes, longer treatment durations, and more diverse populations, including women and children. Future studies should also ensure blinding of outcome assessors.
